title: How to build a diversified ETF-only portfolio in the US
description: Constructing a 'Boglehead' style 3-fund portfolio for maximum simplicity.
content:
You do not need to own 50 different stocks to be diversified. In fact, owning individual stocks often increases risk without increasing expected returns. The modern solution is the **ETF-Only Portfolio**. By using just two or three broad-market Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs), a US investor can own every public company in the world and the entire investment-grade bond market. This strategy, often called the 'Boglehead' approach, costs pennies, requires 1 hour of work per year, and historically beats most professional hedge funds.

Key Takeaways

  • Total Market Coverage: VTI (US) + VXUS (International) covers ~10,000 companies globally. You miss nothing.
  • Cost Efficiency: This portfolio has an expense ratio of ~0.05%. On a $100k portfolio, you pay $50/year in fees.
  • Asset Location: You can hold the stock ETFs in a taxable account (tax efficient) and bond ETFs in an IRA (tax sheltered).
  • Rebalancing: Simplicity makes rebalancing easy. If stocks are up, sell one ETF and buy the other.

Why It Matters (US Context)

US investors have access to the cheapest, most liquid ETFs on earth. Vanguard and BlackRock (iShares) compete to lower fees, resulting in products that are virtually free to hold.

The 3-Fund Solution

This is the 'Standard Model' of passive investing.

Fund 1: US Total Stock Market

Ticker: VTI (Vanguard) or ITOT (iShares).

Allocation: 50-60%.

What it is: Every public company in America. Apple, Amazon, Tesla, plus thousands of small companies.

Fund 2: Total International Stock Market

Ticker: VXUS (Vanguard) or IXUS (iShares).

Allocation: 20-30%.

What it is: The rest of the world. Europe, Asia, Emerging Markets. Hedging against the dollar.

Fund 3: Total Bond Market

Ticker: BND (Vanguard) or AGG (iShares).

Allocation: 10-20% (Adjust by age).

What it is: US Treasuries and Corporate Debt. The ballast that stabilizes the ship.

Execution Guide

  1. Open Brokerage: Fidelity, Schwab, or Vanguard.
  2. Execute the Buys: Transfer cash. Buy VTI, VXUS, BND in your desired ratio (e.g., 60/20/20).
  3. Dividend Reinvestment: Turn on 'DRIP'. When Apple pays a dividend to VTI, VTI pays you. The broker automatically uses that cash to buy more shares of VTI.
  4. The 'One Fund' Alternative: If 3 ETFs is too hard, buy VT (Total World Stock). It combines US and International into one ticker. Add BND if you want bonds.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why ETFs and not Mutual Funds?

In a taxable account, ETFs are more tax-efficient (fewer capital gains distributions). In an IRA, it doesn't matter.

Do I need a Tech ETF (QQQ)?

No. VTI is already ~30% Tech. Buying QQQ on top is just 'overweighting' tech. You can do it, but it's a bet, not a requirement.

How often do I check it?

Once a year. Or when you add new money. Checking daily tempts you to trade, which ruins the strategy.
